draft.title: Fossil evidence for evolution
card: A fossil is the preserved remains or traces of a living thing from long ago. Most form when a dead organism is buried quickly in sediment, which slowly hardens into rock.
Sedimentary rock forms in layers. Layers lower down are usually older, and layers higher up are usually younger.
Fossils in the oldest layers are mostly simple organisms. Fossils in younger layers include more varied organisms, and many look more like living species.
This order shows that life has changed over millions of years. Fossils of intermediate forms, with features of two groups, show how one kind of organism could change into another.
draft.remember: Rock layers give an order in time, and fossils in that order show how life has changed.

a.q: What does the order of fossils in rock layers show about life on Earth?
opts: Life has changed over millions of years
Living things have stayed the same over time
All species appeared at the same moment
Simple organisms stopped existing long ago
a.why: Fossils in older layers differ from those in younger layers, and younger ones look more like living species. This shows change over time. It does not show that simple organisms all died out, because many simple organisms are still alive today.
a.clue: Compare what is found in the lowest layers with the highest.

b.q: A team digs a cliff in western Victoria. The lowest layer holds only fossils of small, soft-bodied sea animals. A higher layer holds shelled animals. The top layer holds fossils very like animals living in the bay today. What can the team conclude?
opts: The animals changed gradually as the layers formed
The animals in the top layer are the oldest
All the animals lived at the same time
The animals in the lowest layer are still alive today
b.why: Lower layers are usually older, so the order from simple to more modern-looking shows change over time. The top layer is the youngest, not the oldest. Being similar to living animals does not make a layer older.
b.clue: Which layer is usually the oldest?

wants.brief: A cross-section of sedimentary rock in three layers. The bottom layer is labelled oldest and shows a simple organism fossil. The middle layer shows a more varied fossil. The top layer is labelled youngest and shows a fossil like a living species.
wants.why: It lets the student see that fossils change in order from older to younger layers.

a.best: Life has changed over millions of years

b.best: The animals changed gradually as the layers formed

problems.detail: The intended answer 'The animals changed gradually as the layers formed' suggests that individual animals changed, a common misconception; populations or kinds of organisms change over generations. 'Gradually' is also more than the card teaches or three layers can show. Wording such as 'Life in the area changed over time' would match the card.

a.q: What does the order of fossils in rock layers show about life on Earth?
opts: Life has changed over millions of years
Living things have stayed the same over time
All species appeared at the same moment
Younger rock layers form beneath older ones
a.why: Fossils in older layers differ from those in younger layers, and younger ones look more like living species. This shows change over time. Younger layers are usually higher up, not beneath older ones, so that option has the order reversed.
a.clue: Compare what is found in the lowest layers with the highest.

b.q: A team digs a cliff in western Victoria. The lowest layer holds only fossils of small, soft-bodied sea animals. A higher layer holds shelled animals. The top layer holds fossils very like animals living in the bay today. What can the team conclude?
opts: Life in the area changed over time
The top layer holds the oldest animals
All the animals lived at the same time
Life in the area stayed the same over time
b.why: Lower layers are usually older, so the fossils run from the oldest at the bottom to the youngest at the top. Each layer holds different kinds of animals, so life in the area changed over time. The top layer is the youngest, not the oldest: looking like living animals points to a younger age.
b.clue: Which layer is usually the oldest, and do the fossils match from layer to layer?
